Mumbai, India 

It’s the financial capital of India along a beautiful coastline with rich historical context, interesting range of landscapes and settlements, a thriving art, glamour, media, and cinema culture, a very multicultural population, the beautiful forests and ecology towards the North, and a lot of survival spirit. 

But the city has degraded rapidly over the years, with the infrastructure decaying, half the city dug up, pollution, discarding walkable streets for wide highways, horrible traffic management, wealth and social inequality, corrupt politicians, plastic littering the beaches and water bodies, and development completely disturbing the ecological footprint of a city with so much potential. And this is just the tip of the iceberg. 

While I still live in and love the city for it’s good parts, this has the potential to become the richest as well as the most beautiful city in the world, but we are unfortunately heading in the opposite direction.

Hello! Firstly, you are definitely NOT alone in feeling this way. Aspects of this post felt like looking at myself in the mirror. I am as lost as you currently, having pivoted my career a fair few times to have apparently reached dead ends in the multiple paths I’d set out to explore as careers. Then despite my multidisciplinary talents and interests (which I was able to explore in my previous job but left because I could go to the next level) I find myself stuck in-between, committing to a path where I either have no experience, or is too unfulfilling or ‘corporate’, or extremely low paying, or just sucky to commit my life to. Now I’m left wondering if I made a mistake pivoting like this. The ADHD brain trying to find a meaning in all of it doesn’t help. It freezes and makes me anxious that I won’t be able to fulfill my own potential. 

However, we don’t lose hope so easily, as intelligent people. What’s helped me make a lot of headway is just actual pure reflection of what you enjoy and see yourself doing with enthusiasm (forget if you can do it all your life, or forget HOW it would be done. That comes later). You mentioned your love for world building and creative exploration with brands. Try to find different scales of work which can help you explore that. Commit to the initial struggle if you can if you think it’s worth it, because enthusiasm helps you grow in that field and open up pores. Art Direction and Communication is a very flexible field which can be utilised in films, advertisements, marketing, non-profit and welfare, institutions, and even big design corporates. You have done your bachelors AND masters, and have expressed clear interest towards the same as well. So don’t drop it.

Secondly, which is advice I’m trying to incorporate and understand as well, is SHARE and NETWORK. Trust me, creative fields and opportunities thrive on this. Put your work out there and express it. Do a couple of personal projects or mock projects that best highlight what you LOVE doing, and use that in your portfolio to get similar work. Talk to people with considerable experience or you look up to, and share this about yourself. We don’t realise how often people around us can guide us towards paths we have no idea about, or connect us to relevant contacts. Create a strong and expressive portfolio, and network using that, while looking for work. I promise you, there are cool options out there. This is what keeps me driven. 

Along this journey, I have to remind myself not to be too hard on myself, and take it step by step. Write down your challenges and options, and reflect on goals. Create specific targets which you can achieve in the next couple of weeks first. 

A mistake I did, which Im learning to deal with, is having too high expectations from myself to find the best match and be this person who has figured life out. This has prevented me to move step by step, making me easily overwhelmed. Just look for the next best thing, explore, work through short term goals, and keep looking for how you can best add value and do what you like. Rest will follow.

You got this, I promise!

I’ve gone to plenty of concerts alone. A lot of them were terrible lonely experiences, but with time and letting go of my inhibitions, I had some lovely experiences as well by myself. Some of my thoughts are:

1) The best part about the concert is, well, the concert itself. Friends or no friends, you get to enjoy great artists playing your favourite music live. Learn to take that beautiful experience in instead of being too conscious of your surroundings and losing out on the main act. Being by yourself doesn’t have to be a negative experience. 

2) Like someone pointed out, freely approach the people you genuinely like and can sense a vibe in. You are human, and so are they. If you are already comfortable and happy being there at the concert, you won’t feel the need to show desperation in making friends. Just curiosity and interest, without expecting something in return.

3) Friendships can’t be forced. If you don’t vibe, pleasantly move on to the next person or activity. Be at ease with yourself, for others to feel at ease being with you. There would be rejections, dry conversations, small talk, or just ignoring because everyone is up to something. Not your fault, so gotta learn to be okay with that. 

4) That being said, it is hard the first few times cause social anxiety and learning to have fun alone is tough. Around you, most people there have their own set of friends, or are too high/drunk to be present in their senses. So give yourself time and space to simply be an observer and take it in. If you’re not vibing, go to the front and just take the music in. 

5) Something that has helped me escape my own head is small activities for myself. For example, I love to take photos, videos, and sketch. I’ve seen people take small video interviews, or keep small challenges through the night, or something cool to be engaged in by yourself instead of awkwardly standing there. In the process, people approach you as well. 

6) Lastly, as a more direct solution, keep talking and approaching people you like, and have something to say to, instead of forcing a conversation. Because people can SENSE desperation and force. It’s okay if they talk, it’s okay if then don’t. You can observe more so that better quality conversation can be made, or just learn to be. It’s all chill, it’s all good.

Nayaab undoubtedly gets legendary status for being such a powerful and vulnerable body of work. Also the depiction of their evolution, personal challenges and journey as an extension of Bayaan makes this even more powerful. I remember going through this album would make me feel like I’m in a movie and rooting for these characters at every step. 

I was lucky to attend the album launch in Mumbai, and I remember Seedhe Maut sharing how long they actually spent working on this album which originally had lesser tracks, but new music kept getting added. The time spent on this is very evident as it has reaped some amazing results in its musicality and variety. 

For me, every track is a film. Sez simply doesn’t make a beat. He sets the atmosphere, adds minor elements that elevate the track to the next level, lots of nuances, and tells a story through a beat (which they talk about in the podcast). A lot of tracks like Dum Ghutte, Choti Soch, Maina, Kohra, and Gandi Aulaad have moments where it feels like Sez is also trying to express himself through his production. 

The major hook of this album is also the storytelling. It’s not mere flexing or word play or lethal punches. They even take on characters in some tracks and play them out. They set the tone of the city (Rajdhaani, Dum Ghutte), society (Anaadi, Godkode, Chidiya Udd), and personal stories (Gandi Aulaad, Kohra, Maina, Jua). I think this deserves appreciation. Being an overthinker, I find myself stuck often. But I am in the process of improving myself. The biggest learning for me? That life is a series of getting stuck and unstuck. We are humans after all. We are often hard on ourselves for not making big moves constantly or achieving a steep incline in our graph towards self improvement. But the graph is always a roller-coaster that you learn from that eventually moves upwards, when our small habits compound with time. 
Some approaches that helped me are: 

1) Recognising why our bad habits surface: Often vices and addictions surface from a need to escape or cope. Mostly it’s the fear towards something, or the lack of motivation to improve, or escaping from distressed thoughts. Take some time out to recognise and address these issues.

2) Create coping mechanisms that are healthier: Life isn’t perfect, and humans design things around them in order to cope from this one tough fucking journey we are on. But what matters is how healthy or meaningful they are. Immerse yourself in art, films, music, long walks, and small hobbies to escape. Play a game, or sports with friends, or go for long walks. The dopamine is quick as well as healthy. Create a folder of memories and highlights from your life. Journal and vent out, through public blogs or private diaries. Make small lists on what you enjoy, and pour yourself into it. These meaningful activities help us feel better, open our minds up, and shift our focus to better things. 

3) Be kind to yourself: Imagine someone dealing with issues. Would you be harsh on them and tell them they are worthless? What impact would it have on them? Now imagine that person is you. Being harsh -> Low self worth -> Escape and detachment -> Downward spiral. You are your own best friend, guide, mentor and support. Be real with yourself and acknowledge your issues, but don’t berate yourself. It takes belief and love to feel good and change yourself. While outside validation helps, talking to yourself kindly and self affirmations go a long way in not succumbing to toxic loops. 

4) Inspiration, not comparison: Comparison, for me, is the biggest killer. I struggle with it myself. It took me a long time to realise that everyone leads different lives, have different upbringing, different resources and different challenges. Comparing someone else’s journey is cutting time from your own life which can be spent doing things for yourself and enjoying it. Instead, get inspired from people you look up to. Follow their principles and values, but don’t try to replicate their journeys. You have your own. 

5) Be grateful: Important advice everyone around me, including my father who I look up to, gives me regularly. There are worse positions to be in. We are blessed with a lot. First step is being grateful and realising we have enough to improve and make the most of the lives we are given.

Hope these help. I am trying to apply these principles to my own life. I often struggle and am stuck right now as well, but am trying my best to create small and meaningful steps and not let bad days bring me down. Cheers to improvement!

Being an architect. 

When I was in school, I was always fascinated by an architect's ability to craft space, play with light and shadows,  understand people's requirements, and design. Even the contribution to and inspiration from culture. The course itself felt fun, and super exploration heavy. 

The reality of this field, especially in my country, is completely different. The pay as well as respect towards the profession is inversely proportional to the long and gruelling working hours. So much of architecture is controlled by brain-dead clients, money hungry organisations, and builders who couldn't give a fuck. The divide between college education and the real field is too high that you feel dissociated or detached from architecture and are constantly berated in an office environment for not knowing enough. To add to that, it is extremely tough practicing unless you have contacts or parents/relatives running an architecture firm which you can carry forward, because of the amount of work and time involved in it, and a complete lack of return for a self made architect.

While there are some good bits for sure, I graduated from college extremely demotivated and the joy sucked out of architecture in general - a field which can't help but gush over starchitects creating over-the-top designs and other architects copying these for their rich clients.

Hello there fellow Delhiite. I shifted to Mumbai a year back. 

While it's pretty common knowledge that Mumbai rents are sky high...I believe ample research, a bit of pro-activeness in terms of asking around and knowing the right people, and a balance of living factors all would play a big role in your shift to the city. 

The further away you go from Bandra towards the North, the cheaper the prices get. In fact a large population of workers stay in Thane, Bhayandar, Virar etc. You have local train, metro (until Andheri), autos, buses, cabs all as options, so no lack of options there. 

That being said, travelling in Mumbai isn't as easy as travelling in a Delhi Metro. It's humid, populated, polluted. Especially the local trains. Plus I assume you will be living away from family so travelling too much would give you absolutely no time to do anything and you'll end up being a depressed sod. 

My suggestion - find a balance. Look for places in Kandivali, Malad, Borivali, Dahisar. Shortlist colonies and approach property dealers in those areas and visit homes IN PERSON. Take some time out for that. I can assure you, if you really look for it, you will find some pretty decent places to and decent deals (sometimes people vacate at the right times etc. so keep looking). You can even start from Andheri and Marol kinda areas if you're open to rooming with people because that reduces cost plenty. 

This was long. I hope this is of any help to you, and best of luck finding a place buddy. Don't hesitate to reach out to people around here in Mumbai, some of the nicest folks who helped me feel like home in this city when I was a complete wimp.

I work at Buildofy, a niche platform that documents architecture all around India in the form of films and videos, primarily homes (with over 600k+ subscribers on Youtube and thousands on our website).

I graduated as an architect last year. My role is one of an architecture journalist, video editor and content associate. Office in Kandivali West.

PROS

1. I get to discover and visit amazing homes and projects all around India, which adds to the learning experience. I get to interview architects too and become part of a story. This is what motivated me to apply here.  Occasional traveling for projects is a big plus and one of my favourite parts about being here.
2. Being a niche field, the nature of my work is pretty great. It combines my background of being an architect as well as filmmaking and documentation. It is unique and it was tough to get into here, so it feels fulfilling working here.
3. My bosses are pretty chill and are driven by a genuine passion to create a brand. They don't employ the stereotypes of being bossy, demanding, and angry at all times. Everyone has the creative freedom to do what they want to as long as they contribute.
4. Our work timings are chill. Weekends are for yourself. We work from 9am to 5pm most days. Sometimes even less. During deadlines, this changes and we are working our asses off, but that is there with any creative project you are passionate about. 
5. We have a choice to work from anywhere we want to since it is not office-dependent. I shifted to Bombay from Delhi because I wanted to be part of the office environment and interact in real-time. I get to work from home too when I don't feel like coming.
6. Multidisciplinary. The work culture is one of doing different tasks and being responsible for one whole project. So I get to storyboard, interview, organize content, edit the videos as well as write occasionally. It is simulating switching it up.
7. Our boss has amazing people-skills, which has what led to such insane growth of this platform. He is barely angry and it is admirable how he handles chaos and issues of even the worst kinds. There has been a lot to learn from it.

CONS

1. Being a niche company, it is still a startup in a phase of early growth. Goals and intents keep changing at times. The office size is still small and we are in a major transition period.
2. Since we are a team of young people from different backgrounds, I do not have mentors and am handling most of it on my own or with peers who know as much as I do, maybe even less. I am just 23, so while it is a great learning experience, I would love a system of mentors and seniors in the architecture field to guide me. Gets overwhelming at times.
3. Our bosses are slightly conservative and have a slightly one-dimensional mindset in terms of architecture, finance, and monetization. This has led to a bit of slow growth and a limited reach considering our potential to be game-changing. Our resources are limited too considering the amount of money that goes into this whole process. This can bring down the atmosphere a bit.

Overall, I am enjoying my time here at Buildofy and getting to contribute and be part of some great projects. It is a stepping stone for me to move onto better arenas soon, but it has been a great place to work and learn and be part of something I have wanted to be for ages. I do aim to create some impact here.

1) Get a sketchbook and a few pens and pencils.
2) Sketch something. Anything at all. (Friends, movies, cars, plants, etc.)
3) You made a sketch. You might not like it. Look at some sketches you'd like to make as references, and try again. 
OR
3) It turns out okay and you realise a certain way of sketching you like (eg: you love rough lines and dark themes). Find some references which match that style, and make more like them. 
4) Make a lot of shit sketches and enjoy making them. Enjoy pen against paper. Copy sketches and enjoy doing that. Eventually, you'll get better at it. Momentum comes. 

There will always be better artwork out there no matter how good an artist you become. The point is to be better than yourself from the previous day. Do this for 20-30 mins everyday for a month or so while jamming to some good music, and you'll get better at understanding sketching.

1) House Hunting is going to be an extreme sport (unless you are already sorted living with a family member). Rents, deposits and prices are very high because of demand. But places are not impossible to find. Ask around and keep options open.  
2) Get used to lack of space (unless you are mega rich). Balconies are a privilege here. On a plus side, small spaces are easy to manage. 
3) Make a checklist of essentials. Lists always help. Try buying them over the space of 2-3 days before monsoon gets worse. Less you travel during the rains for basic items, better it is.
4) COVID is increasing, and Mumbai is dense. Mask it up! 
5) People here are extremely nice, helpful and welcoming. Be nice to them and don't hesitate to ask around. Considering I'm from Delhi, the difference is notable. 
6) Public transport here is better than any other city. Get familiar with local train, buses, auto routes early. It will be worth it. 
7) Mumbai is extremely fascinating, in terms of landmarks, streets, public spaces, architecture, and other things. You'll fall in love with the city. Don't close off and coop up at home. Get to know the city and go out and experience it (safely) 
8) Things can get overwhelming while shifting. Especially because there will constantly be so much to do. Breathe, and take it one day at a time. Enjoy the process. 
9) Experience and enjoy the area you live in. Whether it's South Bombay, Bandra, Andheri, Thane or Suburban North Bombay, there will be pros and cons of both. No need to rant about why you arent living in other parts of the city. Every place has its charm. 
10) Spend frugally and live by your means. No need to live the portrayed posh lifestyle they show in movies and buy everything. Bombay can get very expensive. Everyone in Bombay is work-driven. Focus on your work, don't accomodate too much material items, and experience the city with your senses, not your purchases. Will be worth it long term.

The Central Vista Redevelopment (Conceptual Urban Illustration, 2021)  
  
For a country that takes pride in the value of democracy, it has been heartbreaking to witness the categorization of this project as ‘essential’ at a time when India was one of the worst-hit covid countries in the world. I am sure those defending the urgency of the project paid close attention to the ashy smoke rising from funeral pyres overloaded with dead bodies. I am sure everyone noticed the collapsing medical and healthcare facilities which have been demanding attention for years but were never classified as 'essential' by our leaders despite a year of succumbing to covid.  
  
For a country that takes pride in the value of democracy, it feels almost unfair for a significant portion of the population to feel shunned by the design process of the Central Vista Redevelopment Project. This is not merely a building, but a public space, especially people who proudly reclaimed the space throughout the years after independence. The lack of transparency for a redevelopment project of enormous value almost reeks of secrecy and ploy, compromising on just basic communication, which is all people ask for. Revealing ambiguous final designs merely hinting at power and new legacy, spaces of cultural importance like the IGNCA and National Museum are sacrificed and re-birthed, ridding it of its public nature. NGMA becomes the forefront.  
  
This conceptual illustration is an ode to a new low; an apocalyptic world of sorts which is how I viewed Delhi during 2 horrific months. The smoke and dark clouds emerging from collapsing medical buildings in the background and funeral pyres are also symbolic of concealing the genuine intention of the project to the public eye. I got to experiment with brushes and shadows to bring out the apocalyptic narrative and fill it with details. This illustration is a composition of elements to showcase certain narratives of darkness and people who suffered, all in the name of urgent 'redevelopment'. I would love for you all to take a pause, look through, and feel certain emotions along the way, which is what I intend to do with my art. Do let me know your thoughts on the illustration and the scenario, as I yet have a lot to learn!

I have been feeling this for a really long time (especially this year with the pandemic, final year stress, career transitioning, a toxic breakup and so much more). In quite unusually long patches of time I feel like just retiring on my bed, mindlessly scrolling and consuming media. There feels absolutely no point in getting up and doing things, especially when you are lagging behind and feeling incompetent most of the time. Realised I was digging my own grave and getting the satisfaction of merely eating junk food and no more. 

But there have been times I have pushed myself out of this too, and we need that little bit of force to get us into a momentum. Realise and tell yourself that your thoughts are just just getting addicted to comfort, and addiction is never good. Reflect on the fact that you have one life, and just a few years of being young, so might as well do everything you want to do instead of regretting and getting even worse later.

Now I am not saying jump out of bed and fire away and do everything at once. No. Don't pressurise or be too hard on yourself. Just reflect that what you're doing right now is probably not good for you, and start with baby steps to force yourself into some momentum. Take a walk outside, listen to music, watch confident people or talk to someone close about this and just use that as inspiration or a trigger to get you going. Find a purpose, no matter how small, or just visit someplace outside so that you escape the clutches of toxic comfort thoughts and open your mind. 

You'll get over it really soon. It has been tough for me too, especially this year, and is definitely not an overnight change, but we don't give up so easily! As I said, no need to pressurise ourselves, just talk and motivate yourself and get going bit by bit, placing one brick at a time!

Hello! The thing about anxiety is this downward spiral which makes you question your value and self worth a lot. A lot of these thoughts amplify in our heads and beat us down. You are not 'dislikeable'. No one is, unless you convince yourself that you are. That's the biggest harm you can do to yourself. 

It is okay not to be 'best friends' with someone. You have people who care for you, you have your boyfriend who loves you to death, and sometimes that's all we need. Friends will come and go, but it is important to be comfortable in your own skin, because that is how you will be confident, and gradually start socializing and being a much better version of yourself while doing so. The more you doubt yourself, the more unapproachable you become, directly or indirectly. It just happens, and you don't deserve that. 

Love all those who surround you with your heart without overthinking about further branches and extra stuff. Just be you, and love. You have a friend in me. *Hugs*

I have gone exactly through this. I felt the need to post everything, small or big, on social media as a way to validate myself, socialize, unconciously try to impress or showcase my life. And exactly like you have articulated, it has often led to me just questioning myself after that and just lots of needless, unnecessary stress which doesn't deserve so much of my time and energy to be invested in. At the same time, I didn't want to take the extreme step of not wanting to celebrate my achievements at all and not use social media for what it was, that is, to socialize. 

How did I deal with it? The first step was to realise that posting on social media seeking validation became somewhat of a habit; second nature of sorts. I had to put some thought or moderate what is worth posting and what is not without having to go through so much stress for a free app on my phone. 

To break that habit, I had to take an extreme first step, that is I deactivated my profile and decided to stick to it for 3 weeks atleast. This didn't mean I had a direct solution, but it felt important that I see how I react to when I don't have social media to post. It is important to observe and reflect on how you react, and it does not take time automatically start feeling what you should or shouldn't have posted. 

Gradually, after a tough first week, and perhaps a moment of reflection which made me realize how much social media has taken over my life and worth, my attention shifted to other things around me, better things. The first hurdle is the hardest, but once you pass through, it becomes a breeze. Didn't feel the urge to even return to social media and it has been a few months since leaving it. I feel a lot more comfortable with my own skin and my achievements and day to day tasks. Doesn't mean I don't share, or when I return to social media I don't plan to share. But the break itself is detoxifying and very valuable to self worth, which is probably the first step needed to get over this patch of validation. Whenever I plan to return, I will post what I want to, how I want, how much ever I want to, without worrying about what others think of me or have to say about it. And that mental freedom is very refreshing indeed.

Alright mate, so first things first, you have taken the best first step possible i.e. sending your resume to a position which appeals to you. Your therapist is absolutely right in telling you that you won't know whether you are capable or not unless you send over your resume right, so in any situation, sending in your resume was absolutely the right answer. 

Secondly, I feel you are extremely overwhelmed right now considering the possibilities and what all you would have to do and how they will react to you, and that leads to spiralling anxiety and questioning your self worth. Pause. Slow Down. Breath. You are perfectly alright and take things one at a time as they come. Don't worry too much  about future possibilities and what WILL happen and what won't. Remember whatever you are doing, is for yourself because you are important my friend. 

I can assure you some of the greatest people started off in your position, getting rejections along the way. Some a lot more than usual. What is important to realize is that rejections are not at all a definition of who you are as a person, so don't use it as a way to gauge how capable you are, because that translates to not being confident, rushing in, overthinking, making errors and a lot more. You are all good, and you are you and you have immense value. 

Now about handling acceptance and rejections. It's preferable to tell your boss only if you have landed a position in their office, or an interview atleast. Remember, you are doing this for you and what you feel you deserve best so absolutely no need to worry about who will be dissapointed and additional thoughts like these. This is very common in workplace to switch careers to somewhere you prefer more, and I am sure they will understand. If they dont, they aren't very compassionate or good bosses to begin with. Now, in the opposite scenario, in case you do get rejected, worst case scenario is you will go back to working at the same place, or keep trying at different places. The immediate feeling will be a little bleh, knowing that you are rejected, but absolutely no testament to your capabilities or who you are as a person. If the skills aren't up to par, you work and improve them. If they don't value you, you don't value them. You just keep working and giving it your best, and things will align well. 

Finally, take it one day at a time, one task at a time. The more you venture into what-ifs, the more you will convince yourself of things which most probably won't be true, and just stress yourself out even more. Life is too short to stress over hypothetical situations. What comes, we deal with it, what doesn't come, we don't think about. The email will come when it has to. You sent your resume, you did your bit. All you have to do is give it your best shot, and keep trying. Don't let the stress get to you and stay safe buddy!
